The mountains give him their produce,
as do all the wild beasts who play there.

Under the lotus trees he lies,
hidden among the reeds of the marsh.

The lotus trees cover him with their shade;
the poplar trees on the bank surround him.
He is not alarmed though the river rages and torrents surge against his mouth.

Who can capture him by the eyes,
or trap him and pierce his nose?

Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook,
or curb his tongue with a bit?

Can you put a ring through his nose
or pierce his jaw with a hook?

Will he keep begging you for mercy,
or speak to you with tender words?
Will you make him your slave forever?

Will you make a pet of him like a bird,
or put him on a leash for your maids?

Will traders bargain for him?
Will merchants sell him retail?

Can you fill his hide with harpoons
or his head with fish spears?

Just try and lay a hand on him –
you will not forget the struggle,
and you will never do it again!

chapter.title: Chapter 41
chapter.p:
Any hope of subduing him is vain, for
the mere sight of him is over powering.

He grows so ferocious when aroused
that no one dares face him.

Who has attacked him and come off unharmed?
No one under the sky.

I need hardly mention his limbs, nor
describe his matchless strength.

Who can strip off his outer garment
and penetrate his double breastplate?

Who can dare open the gates of his mouth
to confront the terrors of his rows of teeth?

Rows of scales are on his back –
rows of shields that are tightly sealed.

So closely fitted are they
that no space intervenes;

so closely joined
that they hold fast and cannot be parted.

Light flashes forth when he sneezes;
like the light of dawn are his eyes.
Flaming torches and sparks of fire flash from his mouth.

Smoke comes from his nostrils,
like hot steam from a boiling pot.

His mere breath sets coals afire,
with the flame pouring from his mouth.

Strength is in his neck,
and terror dances before him.

Tightly set are the folds of his flesh,
firmly cast and immovable.

His heart is hard as stone,
as hard as the lower millstone.

When he rises up, the mighty are terrified,
the waves of the sea fall back.

Should the sword reach him, it will not pierce him,
nor will the spear, the dart, or the javelin.

Iron is to him no more than straw;
and bronze, no more than rotten wood.

Arrows will not put him to flight;
slingstones will be as wisps of hay.

Clubs are as splinters to him;
he laughs at the whirring javelin.

His belly is as sharp as pottery sherds;
he moves across the mire like a harrow.

He churns the depths into a seething caldron;
he makes the sea fume like a burner.

Behind him he leaves a white gleaming wake,
making the deep appear a hoary head of age.

He has no equal on earth:
such a horrible creature he was made!

He makes all, however lofty, afraid;
he is king over all proud beasts.

chapter.title: Chapter 42
chapter.p: 1This was the answer Job gave to Yahweh:

I know that you are all powerful;
no plan of yours can be thwarted.

I spoke of things I did not understand,
too wonderful for me to know.

My ears had heard of you,
but now my eyes have seen you.

Therefore I retract all I have said,
and in dust and ashes I repent.
chapter.h4: The end of Job’s poem
chapter.p: 2After Yahweh had spoken to Job, he turned to Eliphaz the Temanite, “I am angry with you and your two friends because you have not spoken of me rightly, as has my servant Job.

Now, take seven bulls and seven rams, go to my servant Job, offer a holocaust for yourselves and let him pray for you. I will accept his prayer and excuse your folly in not speaking of me properly as my servant Job has done.”
Then Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as Yahweh had ordered. Yahweh accepted Job’s intercession.
chapter.h4: Here ends the traditional story of Job
chapter.p: After Job had prayed for his friends, Yahweh restored his fortunes, giving him twice as much as he had before.

All his brothers and sisters and his former friends came to his house and dined with him. They showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the evil that Yahweh had brought to him. Each of them gave him a silver coin and a gold ring.
Yahweh blessed Job’s latter days much more than his earlier ones. He came to own fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she-donkeys.
He was also blessed with seven sons and three daughters.
The first daughter he named Dove, the second Cinnamon, and the third Bottle of Perfume.
Nowhere in the land was there found any woman who could compare in beauty with Job’s daughters. Their father granted them an inheritance along with their brothers.
Job lived a hundred and forty years; he saw his children and their children to the fourth generation.
He died old and full of years.
